intro: Some English nouns can't be counted: water, money, advice, information, furniture… They have no plural and no “a / an”. In many other languages these words are countable, so they cause very common mistakes.
objectifs: Recognise common uncountable nouns, especially the ones that are countable in other languages.
Use them correctly: no a / an, no -s, singular verb, with some / any / much / a little.
Count an uncountable noun with a piece of, a cup of, a slice of, a bottle of…
Know nouns with two uses (coffee / a coffee, time / a time) and countable alternatives (advice → a tip, work → a job).

texte: An uncountable noun is a substance, a mass or an abstract idea that we don't count: water, rice, music, happiness. In English, it follows four rules.

1. No article a / an: “advice”, never “an advice”. 2. No plural: “information”, never “informations”. 3. Singular verb and pronoun: The news is good. Your luggage is here — it's heavy. 4. It goes with some, any, much, a little, a lot of, little, no, but not with many, a few, several, or a number.

lignes: much advice, a lot of advice, a little advice
How much luggage have you got?
How many luggages have you got?

texte: These nouns are uncountable in English, but countable in many other languages. Learn them one by one: no logical rule explains them.

lignes: an opinion about what someone should do
Can you give me some advice?
The news is on at eight.
bags and suitcases for a trip
How much luggage do you have?
school work you do at home
I've got a lot of homework.
the activity of working (but a job = a position)
a place to live or stay
the things you need for an activity

sections.note: Because “weather” is uncountable, don't say “a beautiful weather” or “What a beautiful weather!”. Say “beautiful weather” and “What beautiful weather!”. In the same way: “Good news!” (no a).

texte: To talk about one unit or an exact quantity, add a countable noun + of: a piece of advice, two pieces of furniture, a piece of information.

For food and drink, use the container or the shape: a cup of tea, a glass of water, a bottle of milk, a slice of bread, a loaf of bread (a whole one), a bar of chocolate, a kilo of rice, a bowl of soup, a can of cola (US) / a tin of tomatoes (UK).
exemples: Let me give you a piece of advice.
Can I have a glass of water, please?
We bought two loaves of bread.
That's a useful piece of information.

texte: Some nouns are uncountable with one meaning and countable with another. The meaning changes, sometimes a lot.
In a café, people also say “a coffee, two teas, three beers” for cups or glasses.

lignes: a glass (for drinking); glasses (for your eyes)
a paper (a newspaper; a scientific article)
an experience (something that happened to you)

exemples: Is there any room in your car?
I've been to Kinshasa three times.

texte: Often English has another, countable word for one unit. This is the most natural solution when you want to count.
work → a job, a task; travel → a trip, a journey; luggage → a suitcase, a bag; furniture → a chair, a table; advice → a tip, a suggestion; money → a coin, a note (US: a bill).
exemples: I'm looking for a job. ✓ / I'm looking for a work. ✗
Have a good trip! ✓ / Have a good travel! ✗

formule: uncountable: no a / an, no -s, singular verb · some / much / a little + noun · a piece of / a cup of / a slice of + noun
prononciation: “advice” /ədˈvaɪs/ (noun, unvoiced s) and “advise” /ədˈvaɪz/ (verb, voiced z): the last sound changes the word.
“furniture” /ˈfɜːnɪtʃə/: stress on the first syllable; the t sounds like /tʃ/.
“a piece of” joins: /ə ˈpiːs əv/; “of” is very weak.
“news” /njuːz/ (UK) or /nuːz/ (US) ends in /z/, but it is singular.
erreurs: Can you give me an advice?
Can you give me some advice? / a piece of advice?
I'm looking for a job. / I'm looking for work.
A position = a job; work is uncountable.
How many luggages do you have?
How much luggage do you have? / How many bags do you have?

dialogue.contexte: A Cameroonian student arrives at Brussels Airport and speaks to someone at the information desk.
lignes: Excuse me, can you give me some information about buses to the city centre?
Of course. The train is faster, but the bus is cheaper. How much luggage have you got?
Two big suitcases and a backpack.
Then my advice is to take the train. There isn't much room on the bus.
Thanks for the advice. Is there any accommodation for students near the university?
Yes, there's a student residence. Here's a leaflet with all the information.
Great news! And the weather? Is it always this cold?
No a before news or weather.
Not always. But buy a warm coat. Welcome to Belgium, and good luck with your studies!

mots: Can I give you some advice?
an opinion about what someone should do
new information about something that happened
chairs, tables, beds and similar things
the bags you take on a trip
a place to live or stay
the things you need for an activity
a part of something; one unit (a piece of advice)
a thin, flat piece cut from something

items: The news (is / are) on TV at eight.
We had (a terrible weather / terrible weather).

exercices.consigne: Complete with piece(s), cup, slice(s), glass or loaf.
Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: She gave me a good advice.
She gave me some good advice. / She gave me a good piece of advice.
I've got two homeworks for tomorrow.
I've got two pieces of homework for tomorrow. / I've got some homework for tomorrow.
My brother is looking for a work in Lyon.
My brother is looking for a job in Lyon. / My brother is looking for work in Lyon.

exercices.consigne: Write one sentence for each situation, with an uncountable noun.
items: You want to tell a friend something good has happened.
I've got some good news! / I have good news!
Your student's English is getting better and better.
You're making a lot of progress.
Your old chairs and tables are broken.
Your friend is leaving for a holiday abroad.
Have a good trip! / Have a nice trip!

exercices.consigne: Write four sentences with trap uncountable nouns: some advice for a traveller, a useful piece of information about your town, and a sentence about your luggage or your furniture.
items: My advice is to visit Yaoundé in the dry season. A useful piece of information: taxis are cheap. Don't bring too much luggage. My flat is small, so I haven't got much furniture.

a_retenir: Uncountable: no a / an, no -s, singular verb (The news is…).
Traps: information, advice, news, furniture, luggage, homework, work, travel, accommodation, progress, weather, hair.
To count: a piece of advice, a cup of tea, a slice of bread, a loaf of bread.
Two uses: coffee / a coffee, time / three times, room / a room.
Countable alternatives: a job, a trip, a suitcase, a tip.
